title: Maximize the Number of Partitions After Operations
statement:
You get a string `s` of lowercase letters and an integer `k`. Before anything else you may pick one position of `s` and overwrite its letter with any lowercase letter, or leave `s` as it is.

Then cut `s` from the left: repeatedly remove the longest prefix of what is left that uses no more than `k` different letters, counting each removed prefix as one partition, until `s` is empty.

Return the largest number of partitions you can end up with, choosing the optional overwrite in the best possible way.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every position with every replacement letter and re-cutting the string each time costs O(26 · n²). But the cut is a left-to-right scan that only remembers which letters the partition being built contains, and 26 letters fit in a bit mask. So the rest of the process depends only on three things: the index `i`, that `mask`, and whether the overwrite is still unused. Memoising on that state lets the 26 choices share all the work that follows them.

## Approach

1. `dfs(i, mask, canChange)` returns how many partitions come from index `i` to the end, counting the open partition whose letters are `mask`.
2. At `i === n` the open partition is the last one, so return 1.
3. While `canChange` is 1, any of the 26 letters may stand at `i`; otherwise only the original `own`. Placing a letter other than `own` uses up the change.
4. Add the letter's `bit` to `mask`. If `merged` has more than `k` letters, the open partition ends before `i`: count 1 and continue with a new partition holding just `bit`. Otherwise continue with `merged`.
5. Keep the largest result in `best`, store it in `memo[i]` under `mask * 2 + canChange`, and answer `dfs(0, 0, 1)`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "accca"`, `k = 2`. The winning branch keeps `a` and `c`, reaching `i = 2` with `mask = {a, c}`, and writes `b` there. `{a, b, c}` has 3 letters, so `"ac"` is closed (count 1) and a new partition starts with `{b}`, with no change left. At `i = 3`, `c` fits: `{b, c}`. At `i = 4`, `a` would make 3 letters, so `"bc"` is closed (count 1) and `{a}` starts. At `i = 5` the string ends and the open `"a"` counts 1. Total `3`, and no other branch beats it.

## Complexity

- Time: while the change is unused, each index has one state, which tries 26 letters. After it, the open mask differs from an unchanged partition's letters by about one letter, so an index has at most a few hundred states (O(26² · n) overall, around 100 per index in practice), each doing O(1) work besides counting bits.
- Space: the memo holds those states, and the recursion goes n levels deep.

## Pitfalls

- When the string ends, the last partition is still open: return 1, not 0, at `i === n`.
- A letter that overflows the partition starts the next one, so continue with `bit`, not with an empty mask.
- Writing the same letter back is no change at all; keep `canChange` when `letter === own`.
- Without the memo every choice re-scans the rest of the string, which is the slow brute force again.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `memo[i]` | best count from index `i`, keyed by `mask * 2 + canChange` |
| `mask` | letters (as bits) in the partition being built |
| `canChange` | 1 while the overwrite is still available, else 0 |
| `own` | the original letter `s[i]` as 0 to 25 |
| `first`, `last` | the range of letters that may stand at `i` |
| `bit`, `merged` | the placed letter as a bit, and `mask` with it added |
| `nextCanChange` | whether the change is still available afterwards |
| `best` | most partitions found from this state |
